anchor: RBI’s annual FLA Census on cross-border assets and liabilities of Indian entities.
argumentsAgainst: The census reports outstanding positions, not merely annual investment flows; valuation changes from price and exchange-rate movements can affect the position change.
The supplied official summary is truncated after the information on growth in other investment assets; no further inference is made.
argumentsFor: The census provides granular information on direct, portfolio and other investments, along with sectoral and trade-related variables.
It helps distinguish ownership structure, investment positions and external financial exposure across Indian entities.
The reported moderation in the inward FDI-to-ODI ratio indicates a changing relative balance between foreign investment into India and Indian investment abroad.
background: The Reserve Bank of India released provisional results of the 2025-26 round of its annual Foreign Liabilities and Assets census on 6 November 2026.
The census covers Indian companies, limited liability partnerships, alternative investment funds and partnership firms with inward and/or outward direct investment.
It records direct investment, portfolio investment and other investments such as trade credit, loans, currency and deposits, and other payables and receivables.
indiaImplications: India needs to read external-sector vulnerability through both inward and outward positions, rather than through FDI inflows alone.
The large presence of unlisted entities in the reporting universe highlights the importance of reliable corporate disclosures and regulatory monitoring beyond listed markets.
Sectoral and ownership-level data can support better assessment of capital formation, external financing and the internationalisation of Indian firms.

mainsPractice.stem: Discuss how the RBI’s Foreign Liabilities and Assets census improves understanding of India’s external financial position. What limitations should be kept in mind while interpreting its findings?

officialFacts.text: The FLA census covers cross-border liabilities and assets of Indian entities comprising companies, limited liability partnerships (LLPs), alternative investment funds (AIFs) and partnership firms with inward/outward direct investment.

The FLA census captures detailed information on foreign liabilities and assets in terms of direct investment, portfolio investment and other investments comprising of trade credit, loans, currency & deposits and other payables and receivables accounts.
Of the total number of Indian entities reporting foreign direct investment (FDI) and/or overseas direct investment (ODI), around 97 per cent entities were unlisted as at end-March 2026.
Non-financial companies accounted for more than 90 per cent of the FDI equity at face value.
In rupee terms, the ratio of inward FDI to ODI moderated to 4.2 times as on end-March 2026 from 5.5 times a year ago.
In terms of market value, listed and unlisted companies had almost equal share in total FDI equity capital as at end-March 2026, however, 96.6 per cent of the FDI debt is held by unlisted companies.

example.heading: Illustration: interpreting a position change
example.text: If an entity’s foreign asset value rises between two year-ends, that rise need not equal new investment during the year: the source explains that outstanding positions can also change because of price and exchange-rate movements.

pocketRead.excerpt: The RBI’s FLA Census maps Indian entities’ foreign assets and liabilities across investment categories and clarifies why positions may differ from annual BoP flows.

question.answer: The census is useful because it combines ownership, investment-category and entity-level information, while its key interpretive caution is that changes in outstanding positions include valuation effects and therefore do not equal transaction flows recorded in BoP statistics.
question.prompt: Why should policymakers use the FLA Census alongside BoP flow statistics when assessing India’s external financial position?

sections.heading: What the census measures
paragraphs: On 6 November 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released provisional results of its 2025-26 annual census on foreign liabilities and assets. It covers Indian companies, LLPs, AIFs and partnership firms with inward or outward direct investment.
The census records direct investment, portfolio investment and other investments, including trade credit, loans, currency and deposits, and other payables and receivables.

sections.heading: Reading the findings
paragraphs: Around 97 per cent of entities reporting FDI and/or ODI were unlisted at end-March 2026. Non-financial companies accounted for more than 90 per cent of FDI equity at face value, while the inward FDI-to-ODI ratio moderated to 4.2 times from 5.5 times a year earlier.

The central limitation is conceptual: changes in outstanding assets and liabilities also reflect price and exchange-rate movements. They therefore differ from annual BoP flows, which are used to record transactions during the year.

use: Use the FLA Census to show the difference between cross-border investment stocks and annual BoP flows, and to discuss how ownership structure and outward investment shape external-sector monitoring.

advisory_notes: The static definition is supported for this round, but broader methodological or legal claims about the FLA Census are not independently established.
The phrase “annual census” is accurate for the supplied release, while its broader historical continuity is not verified here.
The claim that the census supports assessment of capital formation and external financing is analytical rather than a directly reported finding.
“Changing relative balance” should be framed cautiously because the 4.2-times ratio is a stock comparison, not necessarily a flow trend.
“Large presence of unlisted entities” is supported for reporting entities, but should not be generalized to all Indian firms.
The proposed GS3.1 and GS3.4 linkage is strong through external-sector statistics, BoP, FDI and ODI; GS2.7 is a weaker and less direct tag unless framed through regulatory institutions.
The pocket-read headline and deck accurately capture the supplied release, but “maps” is explanatory wording rather than the RBI’s formal terminology.

The statement that BoP records transactions during the year is sound in substance, but the supplied extract specifically establishes the contrast through valuation effects rather than a full BoP methodology.

wayForward: Use census results together with BoP statistics, since outstanding positions contain valuation effects while BoP records flows during the year.
Improve timely and accurate reporting by covered entities, especially outside listed markets.
Assess inward and outward investment jointly to identify both financing benefits and external vulnerabilities.
Use entity, sector and investment-category details to calibrate investment facilitation and regulatory oversight.
